title: Callum and the Crooked Claims
markdown:
Callum was not out slaying beasts. He was the unpaid intern. His work was topping up the enchanted quill ink and keeping the important scrolls from wandering off. He dreamt of adventure, as anyone would at the Heroic Guild, but his days were paper: mountains of it, each scroll thicker than a troll’s toenail. The ink in his veins felt less like heroism and more like spilled coffee. Knights clattered past the window on mighty steeds. He imagined the saddle. His reality rustled. The prophecies in the corner smelled faintly of must.

Tuesday morning a whirlwind hit the hall. Sir Reginald the Ridiculous, the Guild’s star knight, swaggered in looking less like a dragon-fighter and more like a man who had wrestled a rainbow. Purple goo clung to his magnificent beard. He smelled of burnt toast and cheap mead. In his hand was not a victory scroll. It was a scroll of expense claims.

“Right!” His voice echoed like a dropped cauldron. “A successful dragon hunt, naturally. Receipts.” He plonked the thing on Callum’s desk. Inkwells jumped. The scroll unfurled like a papery serpent and felt heavier than a king’s ransom, with just as much dodgy stuffing.

Callum sorted, brow furrowed. “One bottle of Dragon Repellent, Extra Sparkly. Five hundred pounds. Steep for fizz.” His fingers came away sticky with purple goo. “Emotional Support Gargoyle Fuel, three gallons. What in the name of sanity.” His stomach did a wobbly flip. Then Interdimensional Toll Fees. Then a baffling sum for Dragon-Scale Polishing Cloths, Velvet-Lined. Dust motes danced. “Here,” he muttered, “is where it gets interesting.”

The office temperature dropped as if an ice giant had leaned on the door. Petra Grimshaw entered: Petra the Ledger. Her eyes were glacial chips. Her smile was as rare as a unicorn’s tax return. Her office was colder than a frost giant’s handshake; a misplaced decimal could shiver from fifty paces. Her suit seemed to drink the warmth.

“Callum.” The whisper could have cut glass. “Sir Reginald’s quest expenditure is alarming.” She tapped a tablet of grim numbers. “We are over budget. Significantly. The quarterly review is next week. You will audit these claims. Every one. Justify this expense, or you will be permanently retired to the archives. Understood?”

Permanently retired to the archives was Guild-speak for fired and buried under scrolls untouched since the enchanted press. A cold sweat found Callum’s brow. He pictured himself lost among forgotten lore, heroic dreams gone to dust. He did not name the feeling. He sat with it, and then he stayed late.

The hall was silent except for the hum of old enchantments, which usually lulled people and now sounded like secrets. Under the desk lamp he found a hidden clause in the Heroic Peril Insurance Policy. It was not insurance. It was a scheme designed to pay brokers more than heroes. The broker was a shady character called Slick Morty, a name that sounded like a handshake you would wash off. The conspiracy was thicker than ogre stew and less appetizing.

Whispers came from Sir Reginald’s stables. Callum peeked through a crack. The knight was not in armour. He wore a silken dressing gown and laughed with Morty, who was polishing a solid gold unicorn horn.

“The fools will never notice,” Reginald cackled. “That Glimmering Wyrm Scale Polish costs a fortune. Hides imperfections, eh, Morty? Makes even a dusty shed scale look like a royal crown.”

Imperfections. Callum’s heart hammered. He remembered a discarded bag of that polish near the dragon’s lair in Reginald’s own report. He crept away with it. Velvet-lined. It smelled of expensive regret and cheap cologne. Proof, at last, that you could hold.

The next day was the budget review. Petra sat at the head of the long table, gaze like a laser. Sir Reginald sat smugly beside her, gold horn under his arm. Callum stood with his evidence, knees like jelly, the air thick with perfume and waiting.

“Sir Reginald,” he began, small and surprisingly steady. “Your report for the Glimmering Wyrm hunt.” He laid out invoices, the policy, the polish. “The Dragon Repellent was glitter glue, used to make the dragon look festive. The Gargoyle Fuel was for Reginald’s pet ferret, Bartholomew, who enjoys aerial acrobatics. And this polish—” the velvet glinted—“costs more than three hero salaries. It is not hiding dragon scales. It is hiding inflated costs. And shoddy work.”

Reginald’s face crumpled like a discarded biscuit. Slick Morty tried to become tapestry. Guild guards, alerted by the noise and by Callum’s unexpectedly loud voice, took him with practiced ease. Petra stared. For the first time something other than ice flickered there: grudging respect, or surprise that a junior intern had not spontaneously combusted.

“Callum.” Still sharp, less lethal. “You have demonstrated exceptional fiscal oversight. The Guild will investigate Sir Reginald and Mr. Morty. Your unpaid internship is hereby upgraded. Junior Ledger Clerk. A small stipend. And dental.”

Callum’s grin went ear to ear. It was not dragon-slaying. It was not a princess. For an intern who had lived in paperwork, it felt legendary. He had faced Petra Grimshaw, exposed a crooked knight, saved the Guild’s books and his own job. Adventure might come later, once he knew a ledger from a lance. For now the numbers called, and he heard a challenge instead of a threat. He even managed a triumphant wink at Bartholomew the ferret, who was busy trying to eat the gold unicorn horn.
